You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

## task-6345fdba: 26x11 cross-separated tile propagation

Solved current instance. Grid 26x11 with a full horizontal separator row color 2 at rows 8 and 17, and full vertical separator column color 2 at col 5. These dividers create row bands and two width-5 sides. Initially, most cells are background 3; the left-side motif exists only in bottom band (rows 18-25):
row 18: [3,3,3,3,1]
row 19-20: all 3
row 21: [3,3,6,3,6]
row 22: [3,3,1,3,3]
row 23-24: all 3
row 25: [3,6,6,6,3]
The accepted output copies this 8x5 motif into the right side (cols 6-10) and repeats the resulting 8-row band into rows 0-7 and 9-16, preserving separator rows 8,17 and separator column 5. Thus propagate one populated band/tile pattern across all aligned bands/sides; exclude dividers and keep row/column alignment exactly. Accepted output has motifs at rows 0-7, 9-16, 18-25 and both 5-column sides.

Demo evidence: (1) 9x7 input with separator row 4 color 8, top 4x7 motif, bottom blank; output duplicates top four rows below separator, preserving row 4. (2) 23x4 input with separator rows 7,15 color 9; output copies the 7-row patterned band between separators (rows 8-14) both above and below, across all 3 bands. (3) 3x17 input with vertical separators cols 5,11 color 7; output repeats a 5-column tile across three positions and applies a periodic row pattern; evidence supports separator-defined propagation, but precise seed extraction may vary. In solved 26x11 test, populated bottom-left 8x5 motif is copied across both horizontal and vertical subdivisions.

Caution: Separator/task ID alone doesn't reveal which axis/tile is the source. Identify the populated motif and exact band/tile dimensions from current input/demos, then propagate it along demonstrated separator-defined axes while retaining separators. Do not copy unrelated sparse markers outside the seed motif.
Demo (9x17) showed a full-height vertical divider at column 8 and a full-width horizontal divider at row 4, both color 9. In top-left region, the leftmost column carried marker 9 for rows 0-3; cells in columns 9-16 contained a 4x8 motif. Output copied the 4x8 motif from cols 9-16 into cols 0-7 for rows 0-3, preserving divider at c8 and the original motif on right. It also copied the resulting top pattern of both regions to rows 5-8, leaving divider row 4 unchanged. Thus use the populated region to the right of the vertical line as a seed tile and propagate across its corresponding empty region; repeat the horizontal band pattern below the separator. Correct test output (13x29) was obtained by identifying seed pattern in upper-right region (cols 21-28, rows 0-5), duplicating it leftward into cols 11-18 and cols 1-8 for rows 0-5, preserving vertical dividers c9,c19 and horizontal divider r6, then repeating the populated rows 0-5 into rows 7-12. This task's motif propagation may use repeated divider-defined cells/regions; infer exact offsets and pattern from current demo. Verified result was accepted. Do not rely on the earlier memory note's alternate task geometry.
## task-6345fdba: diagonal-wave repetition around a cross separator

Solved test: 9x9 grid with full-height vertical line and full-width horizontal line of color 9, intersecting at (4,4) (0-indexed). Each of the four 4x4 quadrants carries the same 4x4 local pattern when expressed relative to its nearest cross boundaries, with the pattern oriented as a reflected/reversed diagonal wave. Top-right quadrant seed as visible in rows 1-3, cols 5-7 was [[1,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,3,1]], with blank 7s above/left; matching pattern appears in top-left rows 1-3 cols 1-3 and lower quadrants rows 6-8 cols 1-3 and 5-7. Specifically copy the visible 3x3 pattern [[1,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,3,1]] into each quadrant at local rows 1-3, cols 1-3, preserving the 9 separator cross; all remaining cells stay 7. Verified correct output:
[[7,7,7,7,9,7,7,7,7],[1,7,7,7,9,1,7,7,7],[7,1,7,7,9,7,1,7,7],[7,3,1,7,9,7,3,1,7],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[7,7,7,7,9,7,7,7,7],[1,7,7,7,9,1,7,7,7],[7,1,7,7,9,7,1,7,7],[7,3,1,7,9,7,3,1,7]]

When test input appearance encourages an unverified transformation or demos suggest a global operation:
1. Treat task IDs, memory, and resemblance as priors only; confirm current evidence.
2. Without a grounded matching rule, request a demonstration instead of guessing. Seek examples that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Compare the complete input/output pair: dimensions, every changed cell, rows, columns, colors, and output regularities. Do not assume dominant test-object geometry controls the transformation.
4. State a rule that explains the whole demo and verify it against every cell before applying to the test.
5. Emit exactly one valid Continual-ARC JSON action, without prose.

Case note: task-a29c068e has context-dependent diagonal continuation. Prior test: bg8, 1 at (4,4),(5,3), 4 at (4,5),(5,6); correct extension was 1 down-left and 4 down-right to edge. Current instance test bg0, markers 9 at (6,2),(7,1), plus 5 at (7,0), 3 at (8,0), 4 at (8,1). Demos 1 and 2 were unchanged isolated compact multicolor markers. Demo 3 established a 7 sequence at (16,12),(17,11), extended 7 diagonally up-right from (17,11) to top/right boundary while preserving original markers; other colors 2,8,6 remained unchanged. Correct current output extends 9 from its aligned pair at (6,2),(7,1) up-right along r+c=8, adding (5,3),(4,4),(3,5),(2,6),(1,7),(0,8), preserving all else. Two speculative wrong submissions: unchanged grid and recoloring 3/4 to 9. Key lesson: extend only aligned repeated-color diagonal pair in the demonstrated direction; don't recolor unrelated endpoint colors. Each instance still requires confirmation of direction/context.

Pitfall: sparse, compelling test markers can be irrelevant to the task rule. A demo may reveal a periodic or row-wise global output; analyze the whole grid. Balance demo cost against the risk of an unsupported submission. Treat rejection as evidence against the hypothesis, not as a cue for cosmetic variants.

# Continual-ARC demo discipline

## Workflow
1. Parse each region, background, object colors, divider orientation, and dimensions from the current instance. Treat task IDs and remembered task-specific rules as hypotheses only; recurring tasks may vary in geometry and palette.
2. Compare every demo input-output pair cell-by-cell. Identify equality/inequality mappings, output palette, row/column orientation, and unchanged cases. Explain all observations with one consistent rule before submitting.
3. Choose demos by information value. If candidate rules remain ambiguous and a wrong submission costs more than a demo, request a demo that distinguishes them. Do not spend attempts on speculative palette or orientation variants.
4. After an incorrect submission, explicitly discard the hypothesis it tested. Reassess all of the test and demos; do not repeat uniform grids, near-identical masks, or cosmetic color changes. Before a later submission, verify each output coordinate, dimensions, and palette against the rule and examples.
5. Maintain the interface contract on every turn: output exactly one valid JSON action object on the final line, with no explanation or extra text. Valid actions are `submit`, `request_demos`, or `finish` only when the instance is over. Do not use `finish` prematurely.

## Paired-band comparison pattern
When a solid full-width row or full-height column separates two aligned bands, exclude the divider and compare corresponding cells. A common learned mapping is equality => 3 and inequality => the first band's background; determine that background from the full band rather than assuming its most visually prominent color. Horizontal divider: compare upper/lower bands; vertical divider: compare left/right. Confirm the exact palette and mapping from current demos rather than importing this pattern blindly.

## Pitfalls
- A known task ID or memory is not a substitute for current demo evidence.
- Do not confuse equal-cell locations with marker overlaps alone: background-background matches may also map to the equality color.
- A rejection is evidence; change the rule/model, not merely the output's appearance.
- Do not claim success or end the instance until the environment indicates it is over.
